title: Japan’s Asteroid Probe Loses Final Engine—Engineers Deploy Ingenious Fix to Save Mission
body:
Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft, already famed for returning the first pristine samples from a carbon‑rich asteroid, has suffered a critical setback on its extended mission: the last remaining thruster capable of fine‑tuning its trajectory has failed. Engineers at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) have devised an inventive workaround that uses the probe’s remaining reaction wheels and a modest “pulse‑burn” technique to keep the mission on track, buying precious time to reach a secondary target—a diminutive asteroid slated for a second round of sample collection.

The malfunction occurred during a routine course‑correction maneuver aimed at steering Hayabusa2 toward the newly identified near‑Earth object (NEO) 1998 KY26, a rocky body roughly 30 meters across. The spacecraft’s ion propulsion system, which has been the workhorse for its long‑duration cruise, relies on a trio of small hydrazine thrusters for precise attitude control and trajectory tweaks. After a series of earlier anomalies, the most recent thruster failure left the probe with only one operational unit, insufficient for the complex navigation required to rendezvous with a fast‑moving, low‑gravity target.

Faced with this dilemma, JAXA’s flight dynamics team turned to a method previously tested only in simulation. By employing the spacecraft’s reaction wheels—devices originally intended to stabilize the probe’s orientation—they can induce a controlled spin that, when combined with short, low‑thrust bursts from the remaining thruster, produces a net change in velocity. The approach, dubbed “wheel‑assisted thrust,” effectively trades rotational momentum for translational movement, allowing Hayabusa2 to execute the necessary delta‑v without relying on the failed engines.

“This is a classic example of engineering ingenuity under pressure,” said Hiroshi Matsumoto, senior systems engineer at JAXA. “We designed Hayabusa2 with redundancy, but we never anticipated having to repurpose its attitude‑control hardware for propulsion. The solution is elegant, low‑risk, and leverages the spacecraft’s existing capabilities.” The team ran a series of ground‑based tests using a hardware‑in‑the‑loop simulator, confirming that the wheel‑assisted thrust could deliver the required 0.2 m/s velocity change with an acceptable margin of error.

The stakes are high. The secondary mission, announced in 2021, aims to retrieve samples from 1998 KY26, a body that orbits the Sun every 12 hours and spins rapidly, presenting a unique scientific opportunity. Material from such a small, fast‑rotating asteroid could reveal clues about the early solar system’s building blocks and the processes that shape near‑Earth objects, many of which pose impact threats. Moreover, the mission would demonstrate the feasibility of multiple‑target sampling within a single spacecraft’s lifespan, a concept that could revolutionize future planetary‑defense and resource‑utilization strategies.

While the wheel‑assisted thrust offers a viable stopgap, it is not a permanent fix. The remaining hydrazine thruster will still be needed for finer adjustments, and the reaction wheels have a limited lifespan due to wear and the accumulation of micro‑dust. JAXA is therefore planning a series of conservative maneuvers, prioritizing the most critical burns and minimizing the number of spin‑up cycles. In parallel, the agency is evaluating the possibility of a future “rescue” mission that could deliver a replacement propulsion module, though such an undertaking would be costly and time‑consuming.

If successful, Hayabusa2’s improvised navigation could set a precedent for extending the operational life of deep‑space probes facing hardware failures. The ability to repurpose existing systems to compensate for lost functionality not only safeguards costly missions but also expands the scientific return on investment. As the spacecraft prepares for its final approach to 1998 KY26, the world’s space community watches with anticipation, aware that the outcome may shape the design philosophy of the next generation of asteroid explorers.
